extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, writers and scholars interested in fantasy literature
extracted.subtask_description: A broad, encyclopedic overview of the fantasy literature genre: its history, major influences, stylistic features, common elements (magic, creatures), and some critical observations about style and language. Useful for readers, students, and writers wanting genre-defining criteria and background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginary-universe setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy literature is literature set in an imaginary universe, often but not always without any locations, events, or people from the real world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These imaginary settings commonly include magic, the supernatural, and magical creatures; they may be entirely invented worlds or alternate/overlayed versions of the real world. Works can be aimed at children or adults and examples include Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the Harry Potter series, The Chronicles of Narnia, and The Hobbit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic and supernatural elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Magic, the supernatural and magical creatures are common in many of these imaginary worlds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such elements are central to establishing the genre; they appear across subgenres and media (novels, films, games, graphic novels). The specific kinds of magical elements (items, rings, grimoires, schools, elementals, etc.) are part of a work's palette and identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from science fiction and horror
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy is considered a genre of speculative fiction and is distinguished from the genres of science fiction and horror by the absence of scientific or macabre themes, respectively, though these may overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a work is 'fantasy' consider whether its central framing relies on non‑scientific marvels (fantastic, magical) rather than technological/scientific explanations or primarily macabre/horror aims; overlaps and hybrid works are common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience/age orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy literature may be directed at both children and adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many novels originally written for children and adolescents also attract adult audiences. Audience considerations influence tone, complexity, thematic depth, and marketing; works may intentionally target cross-age readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language as creator of place (Ursula K. Le Guin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ursula K. Le Guin presented the idea that language is the most crucial element of high fantasy, because it creates a sense of place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good fantasy language crafts a convincing otherness; Le Guin analyzes the misuse of a formal, 'olden-day' style and warns it is a dangerous trap because it is ridiculous when done wrong. She emphasizes that language which is too bland or simplistic creates the impression that the fantasy setting is simply a modern world in disguise, and she offers examples of clear, effective fantasy writing (Tolkien, Evangeline Walton). Writers should aim for language that evokes place without falling into pastiche or superficial archaism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-archaic or merely sonorous language (Michael Moorcock)
rubrics_metrics.description: Michael Moorcock observed that many writers use archaic language for its sonority and to lend color to a lifeless story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using archaic diction merely for surface effect can mask weak plotting or characterization; stylistic choices should serve the story's vitality and clarity rather than substitute for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolism and archetypal figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolism often plays a significant role in fantasy literature, often through the use of archetypal figures inspired by earlier texts or folklore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolic elements and archetypes can help fantasy fulfill psychological or social functions; effective works update or reinterpret these archetypes to speak to contemporary societies. Consider how symbols operate thematically rather than relying on them as mere decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character voice appropriateness (example: villain's language)
rubrics_metrics.description: In various forms of fairytale fantasy, even the villain's language might be inappropriate if vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match register and diction to subgenre, tone, and narrative purpose; ensure character speech and narrative voice suit the world and conventions of the particular type of fantasy being written (e.g., fairy‑tale voice vs. gritty urban fantasy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invented-world construction / worldbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Some fantasy sets stories in an entirely invented world (William Morris and subsequent authors); fantasy authors often 'create his [or her] own realm of pure imagination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worldbuilding should create internal coherence and a sense of place that supports the narrative; inventiveness, depth, and consistency of world rules (society, history, magic) are criteria by which fantasy worlds are judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic system type (hard vs soft)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magic systems in fantasy can be 'hard' or 'soft' (listed as a distinguishing feature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a hard (rules-based, explicable) versus soft (mysterious, undefined) magic system shapes plot mechanics, limits, and reader expectations; evaluate whether the chosen approach serves story stakes and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of myth, folklore, and retellings
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy frequently draws on classical mythology, folklore, epic cycles, and collections (e.g., Homer, Virgil, Panchatantra, Arabian Nights, Celtic and Norse traditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may retell, adapt, or mine myths and folklore for themes, motifs, and archetypes; consider how faithfully to source material, how to transform it for a modern audience, and whether retelling adds fresh insight or merely recycles tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of medieval/romance motifs and medievalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Romanticism's interest in medievalism provided many motifs to modern fantasy; the modern image of 'medieval' evokes knights, distressed damsels, dragons, and other romantic tropes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employing medieval/romance motifs carries genre expectations (chivalry, quests, courtly elements); authors should be deliberate about invoking these motifs and consider whether to subvert, update, or replicate them to achieve intended effects.
